ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a relaxed, collegial videoconference style: turns are mostly short to medium in casual chat and Q&A, while speakers deliver long, structured presentation turns. Overlap and quick backchannels (“yeah,” “right,” “okay,” laughter-like reactions) are frequent, especially during introductions and transitions, with occasional interrupted or abandoned starts. Participants use many fillers and hedges—“um,” “I think,” “sort of,” “maybe,” “you know,” “I guess”—and formulate questions incrementally, often prefacing them as “quick,” “naive,” or “good” questions before adding several clauses. Formality is mixed: friendly banter and personal asides coexist with conventional host language, praise, and technical discussion. Challenges are indirect and collaborative, framed as extensions, uncertainties, or requests for clarification rather than disagreement; answers commonly acknowledge limits, restate the question, and think aloud. Speech includes repetitions, self-corrections, run-on phrasing, and occasional audio/transcription roughness, giving it an informal, spontaneous feel.

Meeting style for this meeting (round_robin_updates): Each person takes a turn reporting what they have done since last time. Updates are fairly long and mostly uninterrupted. There are a few clarifying questions between updates and little cross-talk. The discussion that does happen is brief.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - Okay, mine. I got through most of the interviews, I think fourteen of twenty, and the rest are scheduled for the following two weeks.
  - Fourteen, nice. Were those all from the first batch?
  - Most of them. A couple were referrals.
Opening: Start with one person apologizing for being a couple of minutes late and asking where the group has got to.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Deciding how to restore a degraded tidal marsh so it both recovers native vegetation and reduces storm-surge damage to nearby homes.

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Chen
speakers.background: Doctoral researcher in coastal wetland ecology with six years of field and analytical experience in tidal-marsh restoration. Her work combines vegetation transects, RTK elevation surveys, porewater salinity sampling, invasive Phragmites mapping, and comparisons with nearby reference marshes to identify conditions associated with native high-marsh recovery. She has worked on monitoring plans for small municipal restoration projects but has limited experience translating ecological thresholds into engineered design specifications.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Chen frames the Bayhaven decision as rebuilding the site conditions that allow native plant communities to persist, rather than simply adding vegetation or sediment. She argues that recovery depends on an appropriate, spatially varied elevation and salinity mosaic, using the two nearby reference marshes as practical recovery targets. She is concerned that a uniform sediment fill could simplify habitat, miss fine-scale hydrologic variation, and leave some zones favorable to invasive reed. She wants design alternatives evaluated against likely vegetation trajectories, invasive-regrowth risk, and the ability of the marsh to retain a range of high-marsh habitats over time.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

speakers.name: Eng. Rafael Ortiz
speakers.background: Coastal and environmental research engineer with nine years of experience developing hydrodynamic and wave-transformation models for shoreline projects, including living-shoreline, berm, and marsh-edge designs. He has built the preliminary Bayhaven model using present bathymetry, tidal water levels, wind-wave conditions, and a 1% annual-chance storm scenario. His work typically compares alternatives through water levels, wave attenuation, overtopping-related exposure, and sensitivity testing of uncertain physical inputs.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Ortiz treats the restoration as a coupled flood-risk and coastal-process problem: the relevant question is how changes in marsh width, elevation, vegetation roughness, and berm geometry alter storm water levels and wave forces at the neighborhood berm. His current model compares alternatives mainly by peak water level and wave reduction under the design storm. He sees a wider vegetated marsh bench and targeted berm modifications as potentially protective, but stresses that vegetation roughness, sediment response, and future marsh-elevation change are uncertain inputs. He wants ecologists to clarify plausible vegetation and elevation states and economists to specify which flood-performance outputs are decision-relevant.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Dr. Lena Brooks
speakers.background: Postdoctoral environmental economist with five years of applied research on coastal adaptation, household flood exposure, and public-infrastructure appraisal. She works with parcel-level property data, flood-depth damage functions, stated and revealed property-value evidence, construction budgets, and long-run maintenance assumptions. For Bayhaven, she has assembled preliminary estimates of residential exposure, avoided expected flood damage, and alternative-specific capital and maintenance cost ranges.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Brooks frames the county's choice as a public-investment decision under uncertainty, with benefits and costs occurring over time and accruing to different groups. Her current appraisal compares construction and maintenance costs with avoided expected residential flood damage and possible property-value effects. She needs credible, time-varying estimates of how marsh and berm performance changes, rather than a single design-storm result. She insists on distinguishing benefits accruing directly to Bayhaven homeowners from broader ecological benefits, which may be real but require separate treatment rather than being assumed equivalent to flood-damage reduction. She is skeptical of performance claims that cannot be tied to measurable outcomes, probabilities, or maintenance commitments.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply

seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Hold a planning meeting among Dr. Maya Chen (ecology), Eng. Rafael Ortiz (environmental engineering), and Dr. Lena Brooks (economics). Chen should explain that native vegetation recovery depends on restoring an appropriate elevation and salinity mosaic, using the two nearby reference marshes as recovery targets; she is concerned that a uniform sediment fill could simplify habitat and leave invasive reed favored in some zones. Ortiz should explain that his current model compares alternatives mainly by peak water level and wave reduction at the neighborhood berm under a 1% annual-chance storm; he sees a wider vegetated bench and berm modifications as potentially protective, but says vegetation roughness and future marsh-elevation change are uncertain model inputs. Brooks should explain that her current appraisal compares construction and maintenance costs with avoided expected residential flood damage and property-value effects; she needs credible estimates of performance over time and must distinguish benefits accruing to Bayhaven homeowners from broader ecological benefits. The group should agree that all three perspectives need to be considered and that permitting, cost, and long-term maintenance constrain feasible designs. They should not select a final restoration alternative, quantify a final benefit-cost ratio, or resolve how to value ecological benefits. Keep the discussion focused on the stated site and decision. The meeting should surface the existing perspectives clearly enough that a later assistant can seek externally verifiable literature that introduces a genuinely additional viewpoint; participants must not name, invent, or recommend publications.

existing_perspectives.viewpoint: Restoration should recreate an elevation-salinity mosaic compatible with native high-marsh vegetation and use nearby reference marshes to assess recovery. Uniform sediment placement may reduce habitat heterogeneity and could fail to suppress invasive reed in unsuitable zones.
existing_perspectives.evidence_available: Site vegetation, elevation, and porewater-salinity surveys; observations from two nearby reference marshes.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Sorry, I’m a couple minutes late—where have you all got to? If we’re just starting, I was hoping we could compare what each of us has since last time, and get clearer on what evidence we need before we settle on a Bayhaven concept, especially instead of treating the interior as one uniform fill area.

transcript.speaker: Eng. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: We're just starting, so perfect timing. I've got the present-condition and 1% storm runs set up, and the early sensitivity runs suggest a wider vegetated bench may cut waves at the berm, though I'm not ready to rank anything yet. Maya, when you get to your update, I'd really like to hear what vegetation and elevation range you think is plausible, or rather, what elevation range and vegetation, instead of treating the restored marsh as a fixed surface.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: The surveys really don’t support a single plausible grade. Over fairly short distances, we’re seeing different elevations, porewater salinity, native cover, and reed patches. I’d use the two reference marshes as ranges for an elevation-and-salinity mosaic, not- I wouldn’t copy them exactly. I do need to check the datum alignment and sediment conditions before putting hard numbers on that. Rafael, does the model represent a patchy mixed-height surface at all, or is it effectively a uniform vegetated bench?

transcript.speaker: Eng. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: Right now it’s more like a uniform bench, or a few broad zones, than the fine mosaic you’re describing. I can represent patches with different roughness and elevation, but I’d want your plausible ranges before I- before we treat the patch map as predictive. Do those reference marshes show the elevation differences persisting from season to season, or are they shifting around a lot?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: They do persist in the broad sense. The reference sites keep distinct higher and lower plant zones across seasons, but the exact edges move with water levels and growing conditions. So I’d give you bands and patch sizes, not a fixed little map. I’m still checking whether Bayhaven’s tidal datum... whether that makes those elevation bands directly comparable.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lena Brooks
transcript.text: That range-based approach is what I need for the appraisal. Rafael, could the runs give us outcomes under a few plausible marsh-condition and berm-maintenance states over time, not just the 1% storm with one finished design? A one-time— a one-off peak-water result is hard to translate into expected avoided damage for the homes.

transcript.speaker: Eng. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: I think so. I can run a small set of condition states, say lower and higher marsh elevations, a few vegetation-roughness ranges, and maintained versus degraded berm geometry, and pair those with more than one storm level. For parcel damage, though, I’d need to understand what depth and duration information your damage estimates actually use. The model can give water levels at the berm now, but getting defensible parcel depths means checking the survey detail behind it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Mm, right.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lena Brooks
transcript.text: For the damage side, I use parcel ground and first-floor elevations against flood depth, and then depth-damage curves. Duration matters less in the current residential estimates, though it could matter for contents and displacement. If we can get water levels, or ideally depths, at enough points landward of the berm across several storm probabilities, I can map that into expected annual damages instead of hanging everything on the 1% event.

transcript.speaker: Eng. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: That’s useful. I’ll need to check whether the berm and landward survey are dense enough to turn modeled berm water levels into parcel-scale depths without making up too, too much in between. But I can set up several storm probabilities around the current 1% annual-chance case, rather than treating that one event as the answer.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: For the ecological states, I’d be careful not to collapse the 45-hectare site into one average elevation or roughness value. The low interior strips and the higher patches may respond quite differently after tidal reconnection. The 2024 autumn storm is useful as a reality check, but I guess the model set should still keep those spatial contrasts visible, rather than imply native cover automatically means the same flood benefit everywhere.

transcript.speaker: Eng. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: I can keep those as broad spatial zones instead of averaging them away, like the low interior, higher patches, reed-affected areas, and the seaward bench, and test a few plausible configurations. The catch is, I need to see whether the survey near the berm is fine enough for that geometry. Otherwise the parcel-depth piece gets more certain-looking than it really is.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: For those zones, I’d want the condition states tied to likely vegetation trajectories, not just arbitrary roughness values. The low interior strip is a good example. Salinity there was closer to the reference range than I expected, but native cover is still sparse and reed is patchy, so I need to check whether inundation timing or soil condition is driving that before we call it a recoverable high-marsh patch.

transcript.speaker: Eng. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: That distinction matters for the hydraulics too. Sparse cover and a recovered high-marsh patch aren't interchangeable roughness states. Maya, once you know if that low strip is mainly an inundation-timing issue or a soils issue, could you give me a couple of credible trajectories for it, like it stays sparse or it transitions toward native cover, instead of one endpoint? I can use those as actual model cases.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I can do that, but I’d frame them as conditional trajectories rather than predictions. One is where reconnection and treatment support native recovery, and one is where the strip stays sparse or reed re-establishes. I need to look back at the inundation record and soil samples first, because the salinity result on its own clearly isn’t enough to call it recoverable high marsh.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lena Brooks
transcript.text: That’s helpful, because for the county decision I can treat those as conditional benefit cases instead of pricing a promised endpoint. I do need to know what ongoing reed treatment each trajectory assumes, though. Recurring control can change the cost comparison a lot, and we need a concept solid enough for the September 2027 permitting-fund application, so...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I don't think we should assume the same maintenance schedule for every ecological case. A trajectory with durable native cover might still need early follow-up treatment, but the sparse or reed-return case could mean repeated control. I'll need to put some realistic ranges around that from comparable projects, rather than imply it's a one-time removal cost.

transcript.speaker: Eng. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: Hm, the range matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lena Brooks
transcript.text: I need to check the county's actual maintenance obligation and whether permit conditions add monitoring or, um, adaptive-management costs. If repeated reed control is a condition of getting the ecological trajectory we model, it belongs in the recurring cost stream, not as some vague contingency at the end.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That feels important. I can separate the ecological cases by likely treatment intensity, initial removal plus short-term follow-up versus recurrent control where reed regrowth remains likely. But I'll need to check comparable sites before I- before attaching intervals. And maybe the appraisal should keep the ecological outcome visible alongside avoided damages, rather than folding native recovery into a dollar benefit it doesn't really equal.

transcript.speaker: Eng. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: Keeping those separate makes sense, rather than letting a favorable wave-reduction number stand in for ecological success. On my side, the maintenance cases also need to include berm condition, because a widened bench may reduce wave exposure, but it doesn't make a poorly maintained berm— I’ll make that explicit in the scenario set, assuming the survey resolution holds up.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lena Brooks
transcript.text: And on the economic side, that gives us a pretty clean set of cases. We can look at homeowner flood damages under each marsh-and-berm condition, with the capital and recurring costs attached to the conditions needed to get there. I’d keep native recovery as its own reported outcome for now. I’m not comfortable treating it as a substitute dollar for avoided household damage, especially while the property-value patterns are still so uneven.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That separation is important to me. I’ll make the native-recovery side- I’ll lay it out as likely high-marsh extent, vegetation composition, and reed-regrowth risk under each condition, not a monetized proxy for household protection. I just need to verify those reference elevation bands before we treat them as the ecological target in the scenarios.

transcript.speaker: Eng. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: Okay, we’re at time, so let’s stop there. I’ll check the survey resolution on my end before we talk next. Thanks, both.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Okay, bye—talk soon.

interruptions, cut-off sentences, or people jumping in
